title: How to Find Your Personal Style in 5 Steps
desc: A practical, no-nonsense method to discover your personal style using your own wardrobe, three words and a simple editing system.

sections.h: Why most people struggle to name their style
sections.b: Most people don't lack style; they lack a filter. Without one, every sale, trend and influencer post looks equally tempting, and the wardrobe ends up as a pile of good items that don't work together. The goal of this guide is to build that filter in about an hour, using evidence you already own: the clothes you actually wear.

sections.h: Step 1: Audit what you really wear
sections.b: For two weeks, note every outfit you wear (a phone photo is enough). Then pull out the 10 items that appear most often. These are your proven pieces. Look for repeats in colour, fit (slim, relaxed, oversized), fabric (crisp, soft, textured) and formality. Patterns here beat any quiz, because they reflect your real life.

Pick three adjectives that describe how you want to come across: for example polished, warm, effortless or bold, practical, urban. Use one word for mood, one for shape and one for attitude. Every future purchase must match at least two of the three words. This single rule prevents most wardrobe mistakes.

sections.h: Step 3: Match your words to named styles
sections.b: Named styles give you a shortcut to proven formulas. If your words are polished, heritage, quiet, study Old Money and Classic. If they're relaxed, earthy, romantic, compare Bohemian and Cottagecore. Most people are a blend of two or three styles; that blend is your personal style. The Style DNA Quiz calculates your top matches in two minutes.

Choose two neutrals (for example navy and cream), one or two main colours and one accent. Your colour season helps you pick shades that flatter your skin, hair and eyes. A tight palette is what makes a small wardrobe produce many outfits, because almost everything matches.

sections.h: Step 5: Edit, then fill gaps slowly
sections.b: Remove anything that fails your three words or palette and that you haven't worn in a year. Then list gaps: often a great coat, one pair of trousers that fits perfectly and versatile shoes. Fill one gap a month. Use the Capsule Wardrobe Builder to turn your palette into a checklist, and the Outfit Shuffler to see how many combinations you already have.

If you're changing careers, body shape or life stage, a personal stylist can save months of trial and error and money spent on the wrong items. A good stylist starts with your lifestyle and budget, not a shopping list. You can request a matched stylist here.

faqs: How long does it take to find your personal style?
With the audit method, you can define a working style in a weekend. Refining it is ongoing: expect your style to settle over three to six months of mindful buying.
Can I have more than one style?
Yes. Most people blend two or three named styles. Your three style words keep the blend coherent.
Do I need to throw out my wardrobe?
No. Start by editing out only what you never wear, then fill gaps slowly. Many people find they need fewer new items than they expected.

title: Seasonal Colour Analysis Explained: The 12 Seasons
desc: What seasonal colour analysis is, how undertone, value and chroma decide your season, and how to test yourself at home.

sections.b: Colour analysis groups people by the colours that harmonise with their natural colouring (skin, hair and eyes). Wearing harmonious colours near the face tends to make skin look clearer and eyes brighter; clashing colours can emphasise shadows and redness. The system is a guide, not a rulebook: you can wear anything, but knowing your best colours makes shopping faster.

• Undertone (hue): warm (golden, peachy) or cool (pink, blue). Some people are neutral.
  • Value: how light or dark your overall colouring is.
  • Chroma: how clear and saturated (bright) versus soft and muted your colouring looks.

The four classic seasons combine these: Spring is warm and clear, Summer is cool and soft, Autumn is warm and muted, Winter is cool and clear. The 12-season system splits each into three sub-seasons based on which dimension dominates.

• Light Spring, Warm Spring, Bright Spring: fresh, warm, clear colours like peach, coral, warm aqua.
  • Light Summer, Cool Summer, Soft Summer: powdery, cool, gentle colours like rose, lavender, slate blue.
  • Soft Autumn, Warm Autumn, Deep Autumn: earthy, muted, rich colours like olive, rust, camel.
  • Deep Winter, Cool Winter, Bright Winter: high-contrast, icy or jewel colours like black, emerald, fuchsia.

sections.h: How to test yourself at home
sections.b:
1. Use natural daylight, no makeup, hair pulled back.
  2. Hold a pure white and an off-white (cream) fabric under your face. If cream flatters more, you probably lean warm.
  3. Compare gold and silver jewellery the same way.
  4. Look at the veins on your inner wrist: greenish suggests warm, bluish suggests cool (an imperfect but useful clue).
  5. Judge contrast: is there a big difference between your hair, skin and eyes (high contrast) or are they close (low contrast)?

Our Colour Season Finder turns these answers into one of the 12 seasons with a printable palette.

Use your season's colours for tops, scarves and makeup near the face. Neutrals matter most: warm seasons look best in camel, cream and olive; cool seasons in grey, navy and pure white. Shoes and trousers can stray further from your palette. For an expert assessment with physical drapes, consider a professional colour analysis.

faqs: Is colour analysis scientific?
It's based on colour theory and how colours interact visually, but results involve judgement. Treat it as a practical guide rather than a strict rule.
Can my season change?
Your natural colouring is fairly stable, but greying hair, tanning or dyeing can shift which colours flatter you most.
What if I'm between two seasons?
That's common. Use the colours the two seasons share, which usually sit on your dominant dimension (warmth, depth or softness).

title: Interior Design Styles People Confuse (and How to Tell Them Apart)
desc: Modern vs contemporary, farmhouse vs rustic, Japandi vs Scandinavian, boho vs maximalist: the clear differences, side by side.

sections.b: When you brief a designer, shop online or search for inspiration, the wrong style name sends you to the wrong results. These are the pairs that get mixed up most, with a one-line test for each.

Modern refers to a specific historical movement (roughly the early-to-mid 20th century): clean lines, function first, little ornament. Contemporary simply means what's current, so it changes: today that's curves, bouclé and sculptural lighting. Test: if it could have been designed in 1955, it's modern; if it looks like this year's design fair, it's contemporary.

Modern Farmhouse is bright and crisp: white walls, black metal, a few reclaimed-wood accents. Rustic is darker and rougher: heavy beams, stone, leather. Test: mostly white with wood accents is farmhouse; mostly wood with stone is rustic.

Both are calm and natural. Scandinavian is lighter, brighter and cosier, with pale woods and soft textiles. Japandi is lower, moodier and more sparse, adding darker woods, handmade ceramics and Japanese restraint. Test: sheepskins and candles point to Scandi; low platform furniture and paper lanterns point to Japandi.

Boho is relaxed and earthy, with layered natural textiles, plants and travel finds. Maximalism is bolder and more curated: saturated colour, pattern on pattern, gallery walls. Test: rattan and jute say boho; velvet and wallpaper say maximalist.

Traditional keeps ornament, dark woods and formal symmetry. Transitional keeps classic shapes but strips ornament and uses neutral, lighter palettes. Test: damask and mouldings are traditional; a classic sofa in plain greige linen is transitional.

Most homes blend two or three styles. Use the Style Compare tool to see any two side by side, take the home version of the Style DNA Quiz, or get matched with an interior designer who works in your style.

faqs: What is the most timeless interior style?
Transitional and traditional styles tend to date least because they rely on classic shapes and neutral palettes.
Can I mix Japandi and mid-century modern?
Yes. Both value clean lines and wood. Keep the palette muted and limit mid-century colour to one or two accents.
What's the difference between minimalist and Scandinavian?
Minimalism is about reduction above all; Scandinavian allows more textiles and cosiness while staying simple.

title: The Capsule Wardrobe Formula: 30 Pieces, 100+ Outfits
desc: A simple formula for a capsule wardrobe that actually works: palette first, then a category ratio, then a seasonal swap.

sections.b: A capsule wardrobe is a small set of interchangeable pieces (commonly 25 to 40, excluding underwear, sportswear and sleepwear) chosen so nearly everything combines. The payoff is fewer decisions, less spending and a more consistent look.

Pick one base neutral (black, navy, charcoal or camel), two supporting neutrals (white, cream, grey, denim) and one or two accent colours. If every item uses these, the maths of combinations works in your favour. Your colour season can guide the accents.

A balanced 30-piece capsule might be: 10 tops, 6 bottoms, 3 dresses or jumpsuits (or 3 extra tops), 4 layers (blazer, knit, jacket, coat), 4 pairs of shoes and 3 bags or key accessories. With 10 tops and 6 bottoms alone you have 60 combinations before adding layers.

sections.h: Build it for your real week
sections.b: Weight the capsule toward where you spend time. An office-heavy week needs more tailored trousers and knits; a creative or remote week needs elevated casual pieces. The Capsule Wardrobe Builder adjusts the list to your lifestyle, season and size of capsule, and saves your progress on your device.

Keep around 70% of pieces year-round and swap the rest each season (linen for wool, sandals for boots). Before buying anything new, ask: does it match my palette, does it combine with three items I own, and would I buy it at full price? Then try the Outfit Shuffler to discover combinations you've been missing.

faqs: How many items should a capsule wardrobe have?
Most people land between 25 and 40 pieces. Fewer is possible but needs very consistent laundry and a tight palette.
Does a capsule wardrobe have to be neutral?
No. It needs a consistent palette, which can include bright accent colours as long as they work with your neutrals.
Is a capsule wardrobe cheaper?
Usually, over time. You may spend more per item, but you buy far fewer items and wear each more often.

title: Dress Codes Decoded: From White Tie to Casual
desc: Every common invitation dress code explained in order of formality, with what to wear and what to avoid.

sections.b: Dress codes form a ladder. From most to least formal: White Tie → Black Tie → Black Tie Optional → Formal / Cocktail → Cocktail (Semi-formal) → Business Formal → Business Casual → Smart Casual → Casual. When in doubt, aim one rung above what you think and keep accessories simple.

Time, venue and wording give clues. Evening events lean more formal than daytime. A hotel ballroom suggests formality; a garden or beach suggests lighter fabrics and shoes that cope with grass or sand. Words like festive, garden party or beach formal modify the base code: same formality, adjusted for setting.

• Black tie optional: a tuxedo is welcome but a dark, well-tailored suit and tie is acceptable; gowns or elegant cocktail dresses work.
  • Cocktail: not jeans, not floor-length. Think a suit (tie optional at many events) or a knee-to-midi dress.
  • Smart casual: one smart piece plus one casual piece, for example dark jeans with a blazer.
  • Festive attire: cocktail formality plus sparkle, velvet or seasonal colour.

Ask the host directly; it's normal. Otherwise choose dark colours, good fit and polished shoes, which read correctly across several codes. Our Dress Code Decoder gives a quick outfit formula for each code, and you can get help styling a specific event.

faqs: Can I wear black to a wedding?
In most Western contexts, yes, especially for evening and formal weddings, but check cultural and family expectations first.
What does 'semi-formal' mean?
It's usually treated as cocktail attire: suits and knee-to-midi dresses.
Is a suit acceptable for black tie?
Only if the invitation says 'black tie optional'. For strict black tie, wear a tuxedo or formal gown.

title: Face Shapes and Haircuts: A Practical Matching Guide
desc: How to measure your face shape and which haircuts, fringes and lengths balance each one.

sections.b: Pull hair back and use a soft tape measure or a photo taken straight-on. Measure forehead width (across the widest part), cheekbone width, jaw width (from below one ear to the chin, doubled) and face length (hairline to chin). Note whether your jaw is rounded, square or pointed. The Face Shape Finder does the maths for you.

sections.h: The six shapes and what balances them
sections.b:
• Oval: length about 1.5× width, gently rounded jaw. Most cuts work; try a bob or curtain bangs.
  • Round: similar length and width, soft jaw. Add height and length: long layers, side parts, a textured crop with volume on top.
  • Square: strong, angular jaw, similar widths. Soften with layers, waves and curtain bangs; avoid blunt jaw-length cuts.
  • Oblong (rectangle): length clearly longer than width. Add width: fringes, waves, shoulder-length cuts.
  • Heart: wide forehead, narrow pointed chin. Balance with chin-length volume, side-swept fringe or a pixie with soft pieces.
  • Diamond: wide cheekbones, narrow forehead and jaw. Try fringes and chin-length volume, like a wolf cut or shag.

Face shape is only half the story. Hair density, texture (straight, wavy, curly, coily), cowlicks and how much time you'll spend styling matter just as much. A cut that suits your face but fights your texture won't survive your morning routine.

Bring two or three reference photos of people with similar hair texture, say how many minutes you'll style it daily, and ask what will happen as it grows out. If you want a stylist who specialises in your hair type, request a match.

faqs: Can men use the same face-shape rules?
Yes. The same balancing principles apply; men often adjust with top height, fade height and beard shape.
What if I'm between two shapes?
Most people are. Follow the advice for the feature you most want to balance, such as a strong jaw or a long face.
Do glasses follow the same rules?
Broadly, yes: contrast your face shape. Angular frames suit round faces; rounder frames soften square faces.

title: How to Choose Your Wedding Style (Before You Book Anything)
desc: Pick a wedding style that fits your venue, budget and personalities, so every vendor decision gets easier.

sections.b: Vendors work faster and quote more accurately when you can name your style and palette. Deciding early prevents mismatched purchases: a rustic table setting won't sit comfortably in a modern gallery venue.

1. Where do you feel most like yourselves? A ballroom, a barn, a beach, a gallery, a garden?
  2. How formal is your crowd? Black tie, cocktail or relaxed?
  3. What's the budget split? Venue and catering usually take the largest share; style choices shape the remainder.

sections.h: Four styles and their natural venues
sections.b:
• Classic Elegant: hotels, ballrooms, historic houses.
  • Rustic Barn: farms, barns, vineyards.
  • Boho: meadows, deserts, beaches, festival-style sites.
  • Modern Minimalist: galleries, lofts, architectural venues.

Choose three colours: a base (often ivory or white), a main colour and an accent. The Palette Generator builds harmonious schemes from one colour. Share the hex codes with your florist, stationer and planner.
Set a dress code that matches your venue (see Dress Codes Decoded), then brief vendors with a one-page style summary. If you'd like a planner or stylist who specialises in your look, request a match.

faqs: Can we mix two wedding styles?
Yes. Popular blends include boho-rustic and modern-classic. Keep the palette consistent to tie them together.
When should we choose our wedding style?
Before booking the venue if possible, or immediately after. It guides every later decision.
Do guests need to follow our style?
Only through the dress code. State it clearly on the invitation and website.
